\section[il rimedio]{il rimedio — the remedy, the cure}

\label{lesson:IT-C355-rimedio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to favour, then the Italian for to allow.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il rimedio}
\textbf{il rimedio} — \textquotedblleft{}the remedy, the cure\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il tè con il miele è un buon rimedio per la tosse.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Tea with honey is a good remedy for a cough.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Porre rimedio a} — to put right. \emph{Non c'è rimedio} — there is nothing to be done.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{rimedio} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{remedium} \textquotedblleft{}a cure, a remedy\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{re-} and \emph{medērī} \textquotedblleft{}to heal\textquotedblright{}, the verb behind \emph{medico}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il rimedio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il rimedio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il rimedio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to favour, then the Italian for to allow, then say \emph{il rimedio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does il rimedio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The remedy, the cure\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sistemare]{sistemare — to sort out, to fix; to put in order}

\label{lesson:IT-C355-sistemare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to allow, then the Italian for the remedy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sistemare}
\textbf{sistemare} — \textquotedblleft{}to sort out, to fix; to put in order\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Non preoccuparti, sistemo tutto io.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Do not worry, I will sort everything out.}
\end{quote}

Very frequent in speech. \emph{Sistemarsi} — to settle down, to find a job or a home.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sistemare} is built on \emph{sistema} \textquotedblleft{}system\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{systēma}, from Greek \emph{sýstēma} \textquotedblleft{}a whole made of parts\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{synistánai} \textquotedblleft{}to set together\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sistemare}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{sistemare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to allow, then the Italian for the remedy, then say \emph{sistemare} again

\section[aggravare]{aggravare — to make worse, to aggravate}

\label{lesson:IT-C355-aggravare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the remedy, then the Italian for to sort out.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aggravare}
\textbf{aggravare} — \textquotedblleft{}to make worse, to aggravate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Se non ti riposi, aggravi la situazione.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{If you do not rest, you will make the situation worse.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Aggravarsi} — to get worse: \emph{la situazione si è aggravata}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aggravare} is inherited from Latin \emph{aggravāre} \textquotedblleft{}to increase the weight of, to make worse\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built from \emph{ad} and \emph{gravis} \textquotedblleft{}heavy\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[attenuare]{attenuare — to soften, to lessen, to ease}

\label{lesson:IT-C355-attenuare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to sort out, then the Italian for to make worse.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: attenuare}
\textbf{attenuare} — \textquotedblleft{}to soften, to lessen, to ease\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Questa crema attenua il dolore.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{This cream eases the pain.}
\end{quote}

For pain, light, noise or blame: \emph{attenuare le colpe}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{attenuare} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{attenuāre} \textquotedblleft{}to make thin, to weaken\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built from \emph{ad} and \emph{tenuis} \textquotedblleft{}thin\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[compensare]{compensare — to make up for, to compensate}

\label{lesson:IT-C355-compensare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to make worse, then the Italian for to soften.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: compensare}
\textbf{compensare} — \textquotedblleft{}to make up for, to compensate\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il panorama compensa la fatica del viaggio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The view makes up for the tiring journey.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Compensare la mancanza di qualcosa}. The noun \emph{compenso} is a fee for work.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{compensare} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{compēnsāre} \textquotedblleft{}to weigh one thing against another, to balance\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{pēnsāre} \textquotedblleft{}to weigh\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{pendere} \textquotedblleft{}to hang, to weigh\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
